statement: In laboratory tests of urine fentanyl test strips on dissolved samples that contained no fentanyl, compared with laboratory analysis or known content, strips sometimes read positive, mostly with strong solutions of a few other drugs. Among 104 police-seized samples without fentanyl by earlier GC/MS, one brand (BTNX Rapid Response) read positive in 6 (1 of 52 in one laboratory, 5 of 52 in the other; specificity 94.2%, editors' Wilson 95% CI 88.0–97.3%, so about 6 in 100 read falsely positive); the five described held only buprenorphine, heroin (two), methamphetamine or noscapine, and because the GC/MS methods were less sensitive than the strip, some may have held traces of fentanyl (Green et al., 2020). In solutions made in the laboratory, strong concentrations of four substances turned the strip positive with no fentanyl present: methamphetamine, MDMA, diphenhydramine and lidocaine. With one strip per concentration, solutions of one seized methamphetamine sample, one seized MDMA sample and retail diphenhydramine tablets and capsules read positive by eye above about 2 mg/mL of material and, by image analysis, from 1 to 2.5 mg/mL, while seized cocaine and alprazolam, gabapentin and buprenorphine-naloxone products read negative up to 20 mg/mL (Lockwood et al., 2021). With pure standards and duplicate strips on five lots, the thresholds for lots obtained in 2017 and in 2021 were 5 and 10 mg/mL for d-methamphetamine, 50 and 2.5–5 mg/mL for MDMA, 100 and 2.5 mg/mL for lidocaine and 100 and 0.5–1 mg/mL for diphenhydramine, while l-methamphetamine (25 mg/mL), cocaine and ketamine (25 mg/mL) and levamisole (up to 100 mg/mL) did not react (Halifax et al., 2024). Twelve other drugs, among them amphetamine, cocaine, heroin, MDMA and methamphetamine, gave no false positive on four brands at 100 or 1000 ng/mL, and ascorbic acid (vitamin C) at 10 mg/mL or more did so on one brand only (Bergh et al., 2021). The concentrations that gave false positives (0.5 mg/mL and above) were 1,000 to 25,000 times those at which strips detect fentanyl (20 to 500 ng/mL; editors' comparison). Outside the laboratory, people testing at home reported fentanyl in 73 of 265 crystal methamphetamine samples and 16 of 93 cocaine samples, against 5 of 97 and 1 of 92 other samples tested on site by staff, which the authors attribute mostly to false positives from how samples were prepared at home (Klaire et al., 2022; different samples, nothing confirmed, not tested). A scoping review lists cocaine, gabapentin, alprazolam and buprenorphine-naloxone among causes of false positives, citing Lockwood et al., who found these negative (Kutscher et al., 2024). How often false positives happen in real use, and whether a stimulant mixed with fentanyl changes the reading, were not measured; ways of preparing samples that authors proposed to avoid false positives were not tested. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Yes, sometimes. In laboratory tests, strong solutions of methamphetamine, MDMA, diphenhydramine (an allergy and sleep medicine) or lidocaine (a numbing medicine used as a cutting agent) made fentanyl strips read positive with no fentanyl present. In one study of seized drugs, about 6 in 100 samples without fentanyl read positive. How often this happens when people test their own drugs is not known.
population: Drug samples without fentanyl: 104 police-seized samples (two US cities, 2017) and single substances dissolved in water at set concentrations; take-home and on-site drug-checking results in British Columbia (2019) as a qualifier
exposure: Urine fentanyl immunoassay test strips used off-label on dissolved drug (BTNX Rapid Response in three studies; four brands in one), read by laboratory staff by eye or by image analysis
comparator: Earlier GC/MS analysis showing no fentanyl, or the known content of prepared solutions
outcome: False-positive fentanyl readings, and the concentrations of other substances at which they occurred
magnitude: Green et al.: specificity 98.1% (51/52) and 90.4% (47/52); 6/104 false positives (5.8%; specificity 94.2%, Wilson 95% CI 88.0–97.3%, editors' calculation). Lockwood et al. (weighed material, not pure drug; one strip per concentration): by eye above about 2 mg/mL; by image analysis diphenhydramine capsules 1, methamphetamine 1.5, MDMA 2, diphenhydramine tablets 2.5 mg/mL (about 0.10 and 0.25 mg/mL of diphenhydramine HCl, editors' calculation on the card); negative up to 20 mg/mL: cocaine and alprazolam, gabapentin and buprenorphine-naloxone products. Halifax et al. (pure standards; 2017 lots against 2021 lots): d-methamphetamine 5 against 10; MDMA 50 against 2.5–5; lidocaine 100 against 2.5; diphenhydramine 100 against 0.5–1 mg/mL; l-methamphetamine negative at 25 mg/mL; cocaine and ketamine negative at 25 mg/mL (2017 lots); levamisole none to 100 mg/mL (2021 lots). Bergh et al.: 12 non-fentanyl drugs negative at 100 and 1000 ng/mL on four brands; ascorbic acid 10 mg/mL or more positive on One Step only; heroin 50 000 ng/mL no effect. Klaire et al. (different samples, unconfirmed): crystal methamphetamine 73/265 (27.6%) at home against 5/97 (5.2%) on site; cocaine 16/93 (17.2%) against 1/92 (1.1%).

evidence.locator: Results › Sensitivity and specificity, 1st paragraph; Table 3; Table 2
evidence.extracted: Against earlier GC/MS, the BTNX strip's specificity was 98.1% in Baltimore and 90.4% in Providence, with 52 fentanyl-negative samples at each site (Table 2); the five false positives described contained, by GC/MS, buprenorphine only (1), heroin only (2), methamphetamine only (1) and noscapine only (1). Fentanyl-negative samples were mostly cocaine (22 and 25), heroin (15 and 9) and oxycodone (6 and 3). Editors' calculation: 51 of 52 and 47 of 52 read negative, so Table 3 implies six false positives, one of them not described; 6 of 104 (5.8%), specificity 94.2% (Wilson 95% CI 88.0–97.3%).

evidence.locator: Results › Limit of detection, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (p. 4); Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 5)
evidence.extracted: The forensic GC/MS limits of detection (3.1 mcg/mL in Providence, 100 mcg/mL in Baltimore) were far above the strip's (0.100 and 0.150 mcg/mL), and the authors name differences in GC/MS limits and undetected fentanyl analogues among possible reasons for the differences between laboratories, so strip positives in GC/MS-negative samples may include true traces of fentanyl.

evidence.locator: Methods › Test substances, 1st paragraph; Methods › Interference study, 1st paragraph; Results › Interference study, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Figs. 2–3 legends
evidence.extracted: One strip per concentration at 15 concentrations from 20 to 0.2 mg/mL of weighed material in deionized water: by eye, the test band did not appear (a positive reading) above about 2 mg/mL for one seized methamphetamine sample, one seized MDMA sample and retail diphenhydramine 25 mg tablets and capsules; by image analysis (test band fainter than with fentanyl at 25 ng/mL), false positives were likely from 1 mg/mL (diphenhydramine capsules), 1.5 (methamphetamine), 2 (MDMA) and 2.5 mg/mL (diphenhydramine tablets). Seized cocaine and alprazolam, gabapentin and buprenorphine-naloxone products read negative at every concentration up to 20 mg/mL. The purity of the seized stimulants is not reported, and the diphenhydramine thresholds correspond to about 0.10 and 0.25 mg/mL of the drug itself (editors' calculation on the card from unit weights of 240 and 250 mg).

evidence.locator: Results › Fentanyl test strip interferences, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Fig. 2
evidence.extracted: Pure standards in water, duplicate strips: lots obtained in 2017 gave false positives with d-methamphetamine at 5, MDMA at 50, and diphenhydramine and lidocaine at 100 mg/mL, but not with l-methamphetamine at 25 mg/mL, cocaine or ketamine at 25 mg/mL, or heroin, 6-acetylcodeine and quinidine at 10 µg/mL, the highest concentration printed for these. Lots obtained in 2021 gave false positives with lidocaine at 2.5, d-methamphetamine at 10, MDMA at 5 (two lots) and 2.5 mg/mL (one lot), and diphenhydramine at 0.5 (two lots) and 1 mg/mL (one lot); levamisole showed no cross-reactivity up to 100 mg/mL.

evidence.locator: Methods › Preparation of drug solutions (p. 2); Results › Selectivity of fentanyl test strips, 2nd paragraph (p. 3); Results › The effect of ascorbic acid and heroin on test results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Fig. 2 (p. 4)
evidence.extracted: All four brands read negative for U-47700, U-48800, U-50488, methadone, amphetamine, cocaine, heroin, LSD, MDMA, methamphetamine, morphine and THC, each tested at 100 and 1000 ng/mL. Ascorbic acid alone at 10–75 mg/mL gave false positives on One Step (not at 1.5 mg/mL) and on none of the other three brands; heroin at 50 000 ng/mL changed no result.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Fentanyl-and-analogues/Bergh_2021_FTS_SelectivitySensitivity.pdf (no printed page numbers; PDF pages)

evidence.extracted: People who took strips home reported fentanyl in 73 of 265 crystal methamphetamine samples (27.6%) and 16 of 93 cocaine samples (17.2%), against 5 of 97 (5.2%) and 1 of 92 (1.1%) of other samples tested on site by trained staff; the study was not powered for these comparisons and nothing was confirmed in a laboratory. The authors think the difference more likely reflects the testing method (false positives with stimulants) than a differently contaminated supply, and that their kit's preparation instructions may not have been followed; this explanation was not tested.

evidence.locator: Results › FTS accuracy and reliability, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Relays that false positives can occur at high concentrations of cocaine, gabapentin, alprazolam, buprenorphine-naloxone, methamphetamine, MDMA and diphenhydramine (references 14 and 16) and says dilution prevents them. Editors' note: reference 14 is Lockwood et al. (2021), which found cocaine, alprazolam, gabapentin and buprenorphine-naloxone negative up to 20 mg/mL; reference 16 (Park et al., 2022) was not read; the review appraises neither.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/_Cross-cutting/Kutscher_2024_FTSScopingReview.pdf (PubMed Central author manuscript; AM p. = PDF page)

risk_of_bias.note: QUADAS-2 high in all four laboratory studies (study cards): Lockwood et al. chose materials that drug checkers suspected, of unreported purity, and read single strips against its own image-analysis threshold; Halifax et al. used single pure analytes and tested old and new lots in separate rounds; Green et al.'s reference was less sensitive than the strip, so some of its false positives may be true traces; Bergh et al. graded post hoc. Counted once.

inconsistency.note: Every study that tested methamphetamine, MDMA or diphenhydramine at mg/mL concentrations found false positives; Bergh et al.'s negatives were at 1 µg/mL or less, a thousand times lower, so they do not conflict. Thresholds differ by lot and by material (pure standard, seized or retail product) and are given as ranges.

indirectness.note: Single substances dissolved in water by laboratory staff, one or four brands; real samples are mixtures, and how often false positives occur in drug checking was measured only in 104 seized samples.

imprecision.note: Thresholds rest on one strip per concentration (Lockwood et al.) or duplicate strips (Halifax et al.) at steps two- to fivefold apart, with no repeatability estimate; the false-positive share among seized samples runs from about 3 to 12 in 100 (editors' calculation).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from these sources; laboratory evaluations of test strips are not registered.

grade.reasoning: Test-accuracy evidence starts high (METHODS §6.3, test accuracy); risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision each rate it down one level, so very low. Rated as worded: that strong solutions of these substances can turn the strip positive without fentanyl, at the stated concentrations, in laboratory conditions; the direction is consistent across independent laboratories (Lockwood et al.; Halifax et al.; Green et al.'s methamphetamine-only sample), so the status is replicated, while the thresholds themselves are uncertain. The scoping review relays Lockwood et al. and an unread study and is not counted. Klaire et al. is observational, unconfirmed and on different samples; it qualifies the laboratory findings and is not counted as accuracy evidence.
